translate_en|mods/Dreams/42/media/lua/sh: Outside an ordinary apartment block, a seriously ill woman is lying on a folding bed under a blanket. She asks me to run to the pharmacy and get her medicine as quickly as I can. I run. For some reason I don't remember the pharmacy or buying anything at all — I'm simply on my way back with the medicine in my hand. I reach the folding bed, and the woman is dead. A car horn sounds somewhere nearby. I turn around — the street is empty, there is no car. I look back: the same folding bed, the same blanket, only the woman is alive again and asking me to get the medicine. I run toward the pharmacy and halfway there remember how this ends. I turn around. I come back — she's dead again.

Music is playing. A girl is spinning around on some kind of water carousel and singing. Every time she passes one particular spot, a shark rises out of the water and gently touches her leg with its snout, almost like a kiss. I start spinning beside her. Now the sharks swim up to both of us. The moment we stop, they sink back into the depths. We get the carousel moving again, and the sharks rise after us as if they know the dance.

I'm walking through a dense forest and somehow know the way even though the place is unfamiliar. Near the middle I find a narrow path leading to a small lake. The shore is round and the water completely still. As I get closer, the skin on my hands begins turning silver, as if it's being coated with fine metallic dust. A glowing amulet appears in my palm by itself. <LINE> <LINE> I hold it over the water. The surface reflects not the trees but other places: a stone house, a field under snow, the face of someone I don't recognize. Each image feels like a familiar memory, but I can't actually remember any of it. A branch snaps behind me. I turn around — nothing there. I look at the lake again, and in the reflection someone is standing behind me. The shore is still empty. The amulet starts getting hot, and I wake up before I can make myself look again.

I'm inside a bright maze with walls painted like a children's playground. Small animals run through the corridors. Some of them speak in human voices and offer hints for coins I don't have. I'm supposed to be looking for the exit, but I keep getting distracted: opening chests, pressing buttons, arguing with a tiny creature in a helmet. Several times I have to run from a huge head full of teeth that's too large to fit through the passage. <LINE> <LINE> I open another door and step onto a quiet meadow. No maze, just grass and flowers. I sit down to rest. I hear birds, wind, nothing else. Then the ground under me moves. It turns out I've been sitting on the back of an enormous dragon. It spreads its wings and rises, carrying the whole patch of meadow with it like a carpet. I grab the grass and fly above the clouds.

I'm lying in bed thinking about the stars. Suddenly the room floods with harsh white light. A round craft is hovering outside the window and slowly descending into the yard. I want to run, but my body won't move. <LINE> <LINE> Three tall creatures step out, with thin arms and eyes that are far too large. I can barely see their mouths. One looks at me, and a voice appears directly inside my head without any sound. They invite me to come with them, although it feels more like an order. <LINE> <LINE> Now I'm lying on a narrow table inside the ship. Weak electrical pulses move across my skin and my muscles twitch by themselves. They shine something into my eyes and touch my head with cold instruments. It doesn't hurt. The worst part is the feeling that they're going through my thoughts like drawers. I try to remember something private and hide it, but that only makes that exact memory brighter. <LINE> <LINE> Then I'm back in my bed. It's dark outside. A small round red mark remains on my wrist.

I'm standing in a forest and know there are three spirits nearby — earth, air and fire. I can't see them, but each feels different: the ground trembles under my feet, the wind circles around me, and my palms become hot. Ahead, a mountain grows out of light. It isn't standing on the earth; it seems to be slowly lowering from above. I start climbing. <LINE> <LINE> Gray balls of mist drift down the slope, quietly repeating, “Forgive us.” I think they must be water spirits. I get closer, and one of the balls opens to reveal teeth. The others change too. Long wet limbs reach out of the fog, with people tangled in them. <LINE> <LINE> I strike the spheres with burning hands, the ground cracks beneath them, and the wind throws them away from the slope. They bite me, but for some reason the wounds immediately fill with wet clay. I smash several hive-like nests and people fall out. When the last one gets free, the mountain goes dark as if someone turned off a lamp. I'm standing in an ordinary forest again, covered in mud with wet sleeves.

It's so dark I can't even see my hands. At first I'm just cold, then I feel someone else's presence directly inside my head. My thoughts start coming in a voice that isn't mine. I want to lift my right hand — my left rises. I want to step backward — my body moves forward. <LINE> <LINE> I try to resist, tense my muscles and hold my breath. For a few seconds control comes back, then disappears again. The thing inside me forces me to kneel. A metallic glint appears in the dark — a sword lies on the floor in front of me. I reach the hilt at the moment my hand starts obeying again. <LINE> <LINE> In the blade I see a reflection: a tall figure is standing behind me, even though I can't see it anywhere outside the reflection. I can't turn around. So I watch only the blade and swing the sword backward. Something strikes the metal. A scream explodes inside my head so violently the darkness itself seems to crack. I strike again without looking. After the third blow I can breathe normally and move both hands again. The sword disappears. I'm left alone in complete darkness, not entirely sure I'm actually alone.

In front of me is a huge project — not quite a document and not quite a building, something in between. A diagram made of hundreds of sheets covers the wall, while workers behind it are constructing a real structure from the plans. Nobody can figure out how to join the two central sections, and for some reason everyone is waiting for me to solve it. <LINE> <LINE> I run between tables, erase pencil lines, draw new ones, carry parts around. The team keeps growing and disappearing: one moment there are twenty people around me, a minute later I'm alone. When I finally find a solution, I discover the left section has already been built according to the old plan. We have to redo it. This happens several times. <LINE> <LINE> Toward morning — for some reason I know for certain it's morning in the dream — the structure finally fits together. We put in the last bolt. Everyone is silent. I step back to look at the whole thing and see that we've built a gigantic door in the middle of an empty field. Someone asks, “Well, do we open it?” That's when I realize I have no idea what's supposed to be behind it.

I find myself in an unfamiliar room with three old friends I haven't seen for years. They look almost exactly as they used to and act as if we parted yesterday. I'm happy to see them and try to ask what's happened in their lives, but we can't have a normal conversation: I hear their voices, yet the words sound as if they're passing through a bad phone connection. <LINE> <LINE> An unfamiliar man in casual clothes enters and points to a screen. A large bird is hanging in the air on it without moving its wings at all. My friends smile as though they understand why we're being shown this. The man starts speaking in a foreign language. I don't understand a word, but somehow I can answer him. Every time I answer, one of my friends leaves the room. I try to stop them, but my voice turns back into telephone static. The last one shuts the door, and on the screen the bird finally flaps its wings.

I'm lying on soft grass in front of an enormous white palace. Two people beside me wear pale clothes embroidered with wings. They speak a language I don't know, and I answer in the same language even though I don't understand my own words. Children run around us, laughing and playing ball. One ball rolls straight through my leg. <LINE> <LINE> My companions calmly explain that the children died very recently. Then they lead me through the palace. Inside are endless corridors, doors labeled with names, and sometimes ordinary household sounds behind them — dishes, a television, someone coughing. I ask why I'm here. One of them says something about a “task” that everyone has. I immediately ask what mine was. They exchange a look and change the subject. <LINE> <LINE> After a while they say I have to go back. I try to stay because it's warm and peaceful here. At the main gates, one of them presses a small paper ticket into my palm, like the number you take while waiting in line. Nothing is written on it. I wake up with my empty hand clenched shut.

I'm walking through a maze. At first the corridors are wide and bright, then they become narrower and narrower. Sometimes the walls move by themselves and close passages. Through windows I can see completely different places: the sea at night, someone else's kitchen, an empty parking lot under snow. The doors leading to them won't open. In several places glowing threads stretch through the maze, and I decide to follow one. <LINE> <LINE> It leads me into an enormous hall. Complicated symbols are carved into the floor. When I step near them, the lines begin to glow faintly. I run my hand across them and feel a weak electric current in my fingers. The patterns turn into animals, then faces, then geometry again. While I watch, black mold appears on the walls and icy vapor rises from cracks in the floor. Frost covers my hands, but I don't feel cold. <LINE> <LINE> Beyond the next door is a round room with a large mirror. In the reflection, a smiling person is standing behind my shoulder. I can't turn around; only my eyes move. I close them. When I open them, I'm already running through a snow-covered maze. My legs are going numb and my breathing is ragged. Every time I stop, an electric shock hits me and throws me back to the beginning. After several attempts I stop looking for the correct path and climb through a wall. It's soft, like a heavy curtain. Behind it is the exit.

I hear heavy breathing in the dark and know they've come. Several enormous creatures are ahead, things I've somehow been afraid of my whole life. My partner is beside me. She looks at me, waiting for me to come up with something. <LINE> <LINE> I decide to pretend I can't see them. I close my eyes and walk straight toward the monsters, using only their footsteps to guide me. Some tools appear in my hands — a short hook, a knife, a flashlight. I manage to get around the first and strike it from behind. The second grabs my jacket and tears the fabric. My partner and I run between them, shouting directions to each other. <LINE> <LINE> The fight goes on for a long time and it's completely messy, with no graceful moves. I fall several times, lose my knife, then find someone else's. When the last creature finally stops moving, we don't celebrate. We just sit on the floor. My partner asks, “Was that all of them?” Heavy breathing immediately comes from the darkness again.
What a pleasant dream I had.

I'm sitting in a classroom during a lesson. Like I used to, I rest my head on my hand and doze off right at the desk. I wake up and, for some reason, decide to check whether this is a dream. I count my fingers: first six, then eight. I count again. Finally it clicks — I really am asleep. The teacher is walking between the rows, and somehow I still feel awkward about getting up. I think: if it's a dream, I should at least try flying. The next second I'm already on a plane. I find the seat belt on my left, look over the black leather seat, run my hand across it. Then I tell the person next to me not to bother me: I'm going to sleep now.

I'm at an expensive party in a bright hall. Evening dresses, suits, colored lights, and beyond a glass door a balcony overlooking the city at night. I recognize famous actors, musicians and designers all around me — in the dream that seems perfectly normal. I talk to someone about food, take a drink, move between groups of people. <LINE> <LINE> At some point a famous boxer I admire comes over. He says, “Come on, it's noisy in here.” We go out onto the balcony. I expect some important conversation, but he starts telling me how he once lost his suitcase at an airport and spent three days wearing the same T-shirt. Then he asks what I want from life. I try to give a serious answer, but he keeps looking down at the street. <LINE> <LINE> At the end he shakes my hand and says, “The main thing is, don't leave your suitcase unattended.” Then he goes back inside. I stay on the balcony somehow certain I've been given extremely valuable advice, although I have no idea what it means.

I'm flying above a bright green forest and only after a few seconds notice that my feet aren't touching the ground. I try moving my arms — I turn. Again — I gain altitude. I get used to it quickly and start circling above the treetops, sometimes dropping close to the branches so I can smell the pine needles. The wind whips my hair across my face. <LINE> <LINE> Then the forest splits into three sections and a small volcano rises from the ground. Cold gray mist spreads across the earth. For some reason I know I can't let it touch me, so I fly higher. Heat builds inside my body as if I'm becoming an engine myself. <LINE> <LINE> An animal and a humanoid creature climb out of a dark lake below, both covered in a shiny film. They look up at me. I nod to them like acquaintances and keep flying. The longer I stay in the air, the older I feel. My hands grow thin and my strength drains away. At some point the air simply stops holding me up. I fall onto a cold floor, already inside a room, and lie on my back with my arms stretched over my head.

I'm walking through a dense forest. Black spiders cover the branches and leaves, some as large as my palm. I try not to touch anything. Ahead I notice an especially large one — its hairy body almost the size of a car, its two front legs rising above the bushes. It slowly winds something living around them, wrapping it in web. <LINE> <LINE> I back away and see that the other paths are already blocked by spiders too. There's a constant rustling of legs across the leaves. I cover my ears, but the sound seems to come through the ground. I take one step back and my legs drop into a loop of web. It tightens immediately. The spiders stop scattering and turn toward me. Several climb onto my legs at once. The web tightens around my chest, making it harder to breathe, while the enormous spider approaches very slowly, as if it has nowhere else to be.

I'm suspended in empty space. No floor, no sky, no sense of my own weight — only darkness. A small light appears in front of me and gathers into a sphere. It flies in circles and speaks directly inside my head. It tells me something about the beginning of the world, not with words but with rapid images: a flash, water, cells, faces, stars. I only understand part of it. <LINE> <LINE> A second sphere appears. The first says everything begins; the second says nothing ever ends. They start arguing, moving faster and faster around me. I try to ask about death, but both answer at the same time with different answers. My head feels crowded with other people's images. <LINE> <LINE> Then the spheres fly far away and become two ordinary points. I'm left alone. I don't feel any great enlightenment — I just want to go back to a room with walls and a floor. I shout for them to come back and explain it properly. From the darkness comes only a short reply: “Too late.”

White walls and a staircase going up. Every step is identical and there are no landings. I'm running even though nobody is chasing me. I simply know there's something important at the top. Breathing gets difficult and my legs hurt, but for some reason I can't stop. It feels as if several hours have passed. I check my watch — only a few minutes. <LINE> <LINE> Finally the stairs end. There's no room ahead, only open sky with clouds below me. I hold the railing because the staircase ends at a sheer drop into nothing. It's very quiet. I take off my backpack to rest and set it beside me. A strong gust catches it and pulls it over the edge. I lean forward to watch — the backpack shrinks quickly and disappears into the clouds. Only then do I notice the staircase behind me is gone.

I'm floating on the surface of a calm sea, looking at the reflection of the sky. My arms are strapped to a small underwater device with propellers. My partner says through the headset that we can begin descending toward the rift. We start the motors and go down. The water quickly turns cold and black, pressure building in my ears. Lights from other devices flash around us now and then. <LINE> <LINE> We switch on the floodlights. An enormous animal emerges from the darkness — we can see only part of its body, and that part is longer than our boat. It barely moves. We get close and take a tissue sample. I keep waiting for the creature to jerk away, but it only slowly turns something like an eye toward us. <LINE> <LINE> Farther down we find transparent fish with their organs visible, white coral, small creatures gathering around the light. We record everything and make up names as we go. The deeper we descend, the more animals look directly at us. They don't swim away — they just watch. <LINE> <LINE> My partner finally says it's time to go back. We turn the motors upward. Below us, dozens of similar eyes light up at the same time. Suddenly the ascent feels much too slow.

I'm standing in a dense forest and can't move properly. There's a bitter taste of grass in my mouth, as if I've been chewing leaves. My next thought — I'm already inside an old tree. The trunk is wider inside than a room, the walls warm and damp. Someone is around me, although I can't see anyone. <LINE> <LINE> The voices sound like wind in leaves, creaking branches and birds all at once. Meaning appears directly in my head. Plant spirits don't tell stories; they show sensations: roots reaching for water, the pain of a branch breaking, how a tree feels a wildfire long before the flames arrive. I ask questions, but sometimes the answers have nothing to do with them. I ask about people — they show me a rusty nail grown into bark. <LINE> <LINE> Then something like a ceremony begins. Flowers grow from the floor, leaves spin around the room, branches pass through me. The voices get louder. For a few seconds I stop understanding where my arms and legs are. Instead of fingers I feel thin roots in the ground. I like it until someone outside starts sawing the tree.

I'm sitting in a cabin on a cruise ship. A tropical coast is outside the window. As the ship approaches port, a parrot suddenly crawls out of my back pocket. For some reason I know it's been mine for a long time, even though I never noticed it before. The parrot looks around and says in a completely dry voice, “I like you.” I ask how it can talk. It says, “I always could. You just never asked.” <LINE> <LINE> We walk along the shore together. Or rather, I walk while it alternates between sitting on my shoulder and climbing back into my pocket. It asks strange questions: what color is today, why do people build doors, where do words go after they're spoken. Then it turns bright pink and starts teaching me its language. I repeat whistles and clicks; it laughs and says my accent is terrible. <LINE> <LINE> I open a hotel door — behind it my grandmother is calling me to lunch. I take one step and end up in a dark basement. The parrot flies ahead, insisting it knows the way out. We pass through several rooms and it disappears. I call for it, open another door — and now I'm driving a car toward the beach. The parrot is sitting on the dashboard, angrily telling me it was a test and I'm an “ungrateful pig.” Immediately afterward it asks, “Are you happy?” <LINE> <LINE> I don't get a chance to answer. It flies out through a door that didn't exist in the car a second ago. I follow and find myself in a forest. Glowing signs hang from the branches like insects. The parrot sits high above me in silence. Then it flies toward a bright point in the sky. I think it's its star. <LINE> <LINE> At the end I'm back on the cruise ship. It's sunset and the ship is moving away from shore. The familiar head pokes out of my pocket. I ask where it's been. The parrot answers very seriously: “Global transformation of feather material confirms the direction of electrical discharge during low-level flight through an aggressive smoke stream.” I nod because in the dream that somehow answers everything.

I'm standing among strangers. They're all talking at once, but the words blend into a hum. When I try to leave, my legs move as if through thick jelly. The people come closer. I barely get away and make it to an old abandoned house. I shut the door and go inside. <LINE> <LINE> In the back room stands a large mirror. At first I see only myself, then an old man appears in the reflection. He's extremely pale, his face covered in tiny wrinkles, his gray hair at the temples braided into long plaits. His arms are unnaturally long, fingers almost reaching his knees. There is nobody behind me in the actual room. <LINE> <LINE> The old man raises his hands. They pass through the glass like water and keep growing longer. I back away until my back hits the wall. His fingers are already near my face. They smell of old leather and dust. He touches my cheek with a cold thumb — and only then does he smile.

At first I feel a faint tingling in my stomach and somehow immediately know I'm pregnant. I don't see a test or a doctor — I just know. I sit on the bed and put my hands on my stomach even though it still looks completely normal. Tears come from happiness and fear at the same time. <LINE> <LINE> Then time starts jumping around in the dream. One moment I've only just found out, the next I'm already waiting for the first movement. I walk around the house very carefully, refuse to lift a heavy mug, eat an apple and wonder whether the baby likes it. Everything around me seems connected to the child, even things they'll never see. <LINE> <LINE> Finally I feel a tiny push from inside. I go still and wait for another. It comes again, a little farther to the left. I start laughing and call to someone in the next room, but for some reason no sound comes out. So I just sit there with my hand on my stomach and wait for another kick.

We enter a dark room. I already know there are aggressive animals locked in the rooms nearby, and we don't have any weapons. I try to lift something with my mind. I close my eyes, picture it moving, open them — it worked. When the animals rush us, I hurl whatever is around at them without touching anything with my hands. Then I stop bothering with objects and lift the animals themselves. They hang in the air, thrashing, while I throw them into the walls.

I'm heading to an evening concert by an old rock band I used to listen to all the time. There's a crowd at the entrance, headlights and signs glaring in my eyes. Instead of pushing closer to the stage, I go to the bar and get a drink. There's noise behind me, people arguing, even a few pops somewhere that sound like gunshots, but nobody around me seems to care. <LINE> <LINE> When the musicians come out, the opening chords are unexpectedly familiar. I haven't listened to this kind of music in years, but my body remembers — my foot starts tapping immediately. I look at the people around me and for a few seconds see them as they were fifteen years ago: different clothes, different hairstyles. I look at my hands — they're younger too. <LINE> <LINE> The song ends and everything returns to normal. The musicians onstage are old again, and I'm holding the same glass. They start the next song and our ages begin changing again, only this time in the opposite direction. I decide not to look at my hands and just listen.

I'm standing among rocks in some kind of desert. Wind drives dust across the ground, and behind distant cliffs there's a rumbling like a thunderstorm. Then I realize it isn't thunder. People are coming from there, shooting, someone is shouting, shells are landing nearby. I have a weapon in my hands, and for some reason I'm running with everyone else. <LINE> <LINE> At some point everything becomes quiet. I'm no longer in the desert but in a clearing. Tall grass, flowers, warm sunlight. I sit on a stump and simply watch trees appear through mist above a river. It's so peaceful that the war feels like something from another dream. <LINE> <LINE> Then a dull impact comes from the forest. Another one. Birds burst from the branches. Mist rolls back across the clearing, and vehicles and running people begin to emerge through it. I jump up and run with them even though I have no idea where we're going.

I'm in an enormous library. In one hand I have a kerosene lamp, in the other a box of matches. For some reason I know for certain that the books have to be burned. I walk to the first shelf, pour kerosene over the spines and throw a match. The fire climbs immediately. <LINE> <LINE> After that I work almost calmly: row after row, shelf after shelf. The hall gets hot, smoke stings my eyes, plaster falls from the ceiling. Voices and pounding are already coming from behind the doors — someone is trying to get in. <LINE> <LINE> Near the far wall I notice one thin book with no title. For some reason I'm not allowed to burn it. I hide it under my clothes and run out through a side door. <LINE> <LINE> Outside I look back. The windows are filled entirely with fire. I take out the book I saved and open it — every page is blank.

I'm walking through a field covered in smoke. Somewhere ahead metal clangs, people and horses scream. I have a sword in my hands, although I don't remember where it came from or which side I'm on. Breathing is difficult, dust in my mouth. <LINE> <LINE> Someone falls on my left, a flash on my right. I swing the sword and suddenly see my palm — the blade passed across it, as if part of my hand has been cut away. Blood pulses out. I shout for a medic, but my voice stretches unnaturally slowly. <LINE> <LINE> In fact, everything around me is slowing down. Clumps of mud hang in the air. In front of me a rider in heavy armor pulls the reins, the horse rears, and every movement takes forever. I have time to see even the scratches on his metal gauntlet. <LINE> <LINE> Then a strange voice speaks directly inside my head: <LINE> <LINE> — If you don't mind, I'll borrow the body for a little while. <LINE> <LINE> — Who are you? <LINE> <LINE> — You. Just the one who remembers a few things. <LINE> <LINE> I try to ask another question, but the voice cuts me off: <LINE> <LINE> — Not now. We'll talk in another dream.

I'm lying in the mud in the middle of a battle. Things whistle overhead and the ground jerks with explosions. I have an assault rifle in my hands, with people beside me just as filthy as I am. I don't know their names or even my own rank, but somehow I understand the orders and run when they run. <LINE> <LINE> Another explosion makes me press my face into the ground. I close my eyes for literally one second. <LINE> <LINE> I open them — now I'm in an early-morning forest. Dew on the grass, pale light between the trees, a woodpecker somewhere. A woman in a gray coat stands in front of me, completely wrong for the forest. She asks: <LINE> <LINE> — Can you still hear it? <LINE> <LINE> At first I don't know what she means. Then I notice it: far behind the birds and rustling leaves, artillery is still rumbling. The woman nods as if that's exactly the answer she was waiting for and walks away between the trees.

It's dark, but somehow I can see myself from outside and realize I'm wearing an enormous white rabbit costume. The ears catch on branches and the paws make it hard to run properly. A person in a black hoodie flashes ahead of me, looks back and disappears around a corner. <LINE> <LINE> Immediately someone starts shooting. I dive into bushes and race through them almost on all fours. For some reason the rabbit paws actually help now. Then I trip and fly headfirst — a broken branch is sticking out of the top of my head. It barely hurts, but turning my neck is awkward. <LINE> <LINE> Huge old women emerge from the darkness. All of them are smiling. One folds herself in half with a loud crack. Then the second, the third. They're clearly waiting for me to copy them. <LINE> <LINE> I try to refuse, but the costume starts dancing by itself. A second later I'm already swinging my hips and folding in half too with that awful cracking sound.

I'm wandering through an empty city. No cars, store doors open, nobody inside. All I can hear are my footsteps. <LINE> <LINE> Suddenly a cold jet of water hits me in the back. I turn around — a hippopotamus is charging at me. Very fast, almost like a motorcycle. Somehow it spits or shoots water and is surprisingly accurate. I run down the street, constantly dodging new blasts. <LINE> <LINE> I see a high wall ahead and decide to climb it. I run up and grab it — only then do I notice the entire wall is made of chicken eggs. They burst one after another. My hands sink inside, then my shoulders, my chest. <LINE> <LINE> I start drowning in raw egg while the hippopotamus stops nearby and calmly watches.

I'm standing at the edge of a high cliff. I can't see anything below, just gray depth. I decide to step back, but the wind pushes me from behind and I fall. I fall for so long that eventually I stop being afraid and simply wait for it to end. <LINE> <LINE> It ends suddenly: my whole body crashes onto an office desk. I'm lying among papers while angular machines hum nearby. I try to get up and realize my arms and legs won't move. <LINE> <LINE> An employee comes out from behind a partition. His face is ordinary, but his voice sounds like an automated phone system. He looks at me and says: <LINE> <LINE> — You're frightening me. Please stop lying on the workstation. <LINE> <LINE> I want to explain that I can't stand up, but start coughing. Dark drops land on the papers. The employee calls someone for help in the same calm machine voice. The last thing I hear is: <LINE> <LINE> — We've got another person from the ceiling.

Heavy rain outside the window. I'm sitting in a room listening to water tap against the glass. Then I notice a person in a long coat standing in the yard. No umbrella, staring directly at my window. <LINE> <LINE> I go outside. The rain soaks my clothes immediately. The person doesn't move and I can't see a face under the hood. I walk closer, and he holds out an old black umbrella. <LINE> <LINE> — Is this for me? — I ask. <LINE> <LINE> — Yes. <LINE> <LINE> — Who are you? <LINE> <LINE> He shrugs: <LINE> <LINE> — I'm just doing my job. <LINE> <LINE> I take the umbrella and open it. Underneath it's dry, but for some reason snow is falling on top of it.

I'm walking over damp ground when I notice a large earthworm moving beside my boot. It raises the front of its body and says: <LINE> <LINE> — Careful, this is the entrance. <LINE> <LINE> Several more worms crawl out of the soil nearby. They're digging narrow channels and arguing about which way to turn. I ask what they're building. <LINE> <LINE> — A maze, — one says. — We lost the old one. <LINE> <LINE> They invite me to come with them. For some reason I become tiny and start crawling through an earthen tunnel behind the worms. Glowing triangles fly above my head through openings in the soil. <LINE> <LINE> — What are those? <LINE> <LINE> — Doesn't matter, — says the worm in front. — Just don't step on the blue ones. <LINE> <LINE> I look down. The entire floor is blue.

I look at myself in a mirror. My face and body are badly burned, the skin black and cracked in places. A second later I'm outside beneath high-voltage power lines. I climb a pole and grab the wires. Electricity runs through my whole body, but there is almost no pain — just a violent trembling inside me. I keep moving along the wires, and the pylons fall one after another behind me.

A heavy metal door is in front of me. I open it with both hands and enter a long concrete tunnel. There's almost no light, only occasional lamps on the ceiling. The farther I go, the thicker the white fog becomes. <LINE> <LINE> At some point a tall faceless figure walks out of the fog. It comes almost right up to me and asks: <LINE> <LINE> — Why are you here? <LINE> <LINE> I think for a long time because I genuinely don't know.
